title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
Conventional Commits

Many teams follow a strict prefix naming system to categorize changes. This makes the Git log easily machine-readable for automated changelogs.

feat: add user authentication login endpoint
fix: resolve memory leak in database connector
docs: update setup instructions in README
style: correct indentation layout in dashboard file
refactor: optimize data processing loop performance
[py,R]: ... (modifying python, R files)
bugfix: ... (all bug fixes commits)
#35890: ... (tracking numbers)

Never write single-word or lazy messages like:

"fixed"
"update"
"stuff"
"bug fix"
"working"
"manifesto"



👎 They offer zero historical value.

title: Intro to Git (part 2)

text:
Avoid Explaining the “How” Instead of the “Why”

Avoid messages like:
"Changed line 45 from x to y"



Git already tracks the exact lines changed.
Use the message to explain why changing that line was necessary for the software logic.

title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
Avoid Aggressive or Emotional Language

Avoid venting frustration in the public history log:
"fixing stupid bug from teammate"




"finally working after 5 hours of torture"



Maintain professional communication.
What if a hiring manager reviews your public GitHub repository?

title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
Avoid Combining Multiple Unrelated Changes

Avoid bundling a feature addition, a bug fix, and a documentation update into a single massive commit
"fix login and update readme and fix style layout"

Can be incredible difficult to untangle.
Split them into small, atomic commits instead.

title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
Adding a .gitignore file
A .gitignore file1 is a plain text file placed in the root directory of a Git repository that explicitly tells Git which files and folders to ignore.



project/
  .git/
  .gitignore
  README.md
  data/
    ...
  code/
    ...
  docs/
    ...

The Dot Matters: The file name must be exactly .gitignore

title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
Why You Need One?

Keeps Repositories Clean: It prevents junk files like system logs (.log), temporary folders, and OS-generated files (like Mac’s .DS_Store) from cluttering your repository.
Secures Private Data: It blocks you from accidentally uploading sensitive credentials, API keys, passwords, or configuration files (like .env) to public platforms like GitHub.
Saves Storage Space: It keeps massive data directories, external libraries (like Node’s node_modules or Python’s venv), and heavy compiled binaries out of your Git history.

The “Golden Rule” of .gitignore


Warning: Git can only ignore untracked files!


If you commit a file first, and then add it to your .gitignore later, Git will continue to track it.


To fix this and force Git to honor the new rule, you have to manually remove the file from your active staging cache using the command:  git rm --cached <filename>

title: Project Organization
text:
Project Organization
When starting a new project, it is worthwhile to spend some time thinking about how to best organize its content.

This means asking questions such as:

What are my project inputs?
What types of outputs do I expect to come out of this project?
How does this project relate to other projects I am working on?

title: Project Organization
section: When you begin a new project …
text:
When you begin a new project …

It is generally a good idea to store all of the files relevant to one project under a common root directory.
The exception to this rule is source code or scripts that are used in multiple projects. Each such program might have a project directory of its own.

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules

Raw data should never be changed. Save it into a data/ folder and treat it as immutable.
The processed, clean version of your data will go into a dedicated file or directory, e.g., clean_data.json or processed_data/.
Anything that can be generated from code goes into its own folder.

output/, results/, images/

If there are text documents, put them in their own folder:

docs/

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules (cont’d)

Code also has its own folder: code/.

If you write a lot of functions, then create a functions/ folder
Or also a src/ (for source) folder to save processing/analysis code.

If processing/analysis scripts are meant to be used in a certain order, you can number them:

e.g., script1-data-prepration.R, script2-exploratory-analysis.R, script3-regression-model.R, etc.

Sometimes the pipeline is not linear but branched, so numbering may not always make sense.
Modularize your code: split a giant script into short, single-purpose scripts with well-defined inputs and outputs.

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules (cont’d)

A project directory should be a portable island.
It can be zipped up, moved to a different folder, sent to a colleague, or cloned onto a remote server …
… and every script still runs without modifying a single line of code.

title: Project Organization
text:
Documentation (README files)

Each of your projects should always be accompanied by a README file.
The README should contain all the information an outsider would need to understand what the project is all about:

what are the inputs
what are the outputs,
where to find files within the project directory, etc.

The README is simply a text file, there’s nothing special to it.

I like to write it in markdown syntax: README.md

Writing down everything about a project in a README.md can be tedious, but it pays off.

title: Project Organization
text:
README file(s)

Record who the author/s is/are,
the date the project was started,
a description of what the project is for,
describe important details
(a README file is sort of a growing/living document)


Get in the habit of starting a project by creating a README file.
Also, you can include README files inside the project’s directories: e.g. a README for the data/ folder, or for the docs/ filder.

title: Project Organization
text:
Some Comments

How you define a project is largely up to you.
It could be all the work you do on a given dataset,
Or all the work you do for a thesis or dissertation,
Or each manuscript could be its own project even if it uses the same dataset as a different project.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Reading

Title: Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research
Author(s): Sandve G.K., Nekrutenki A., Taylor J., Hovig E.
Year: 2013
Journal: PLOS Computational Biology 9(10): e1003285
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Why are we here?

Beyond Morality: Reproducibility isn’t just a moral obligation to your field; a lack of tracking is a direct technical burden on you.
The Time-Saver: Meticulous tracking allows your future self to effortlessly apply past methods to new data or reuse code templates across separate projects.
The Bare-Minimum Threshold: At an absolute baseline, you must at least be able to reproduce your own results to defend your science against future questioning.
The Reality Check: Because any given analysis contains an exponential combination of parameters and software variables, memory will fail you. You must record details while underway.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Rules 1 & 2: Eliminating Human Drift

The Documentation Trap: Manual logs easily drift out of sync.
The Executable Solution: Write your entire workflow as a directly executable file—such as a shell script or a Makefile.
Ban Manual Clicks: Avoid manual copy-pasting, mouse clicks or graphical format tweaks between documents.


Rules 3 & 4: Freezing Your Software State

The Version Lock: Minor changes between software updates can alter data outputs or prevent code from running entirely.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
section: Rule 5: Exposing the Pipeline’s Inner Mechanics
text:
Rule 5: Exposing the Pipeline’s Inner Mechanics




The Analytical Value
Quickly browsing through step-by-step intermediate output files can reveal silent logical discrepancies, catching bugs that are completely masked in final summary charts.

The Pipeline Value
If your full project execution is long or resource-heavy, archiving standardized intermediate states allows you to re-run localized parts of the process without starting over from scratch.


The Audit Baseline: Storing intermediate files allows external peers to critically examine your complete pipeline logic without needing all your local executables operational.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Rules 6 & 7: Perfect Replications & Data Foundations






Rule 6: The Random Seed Mandate


Many analyses involve stochastic element randomness. To achieve an exact procedural reproduction rather than just an approximation, you must explicitly record and pass your initial random seed.




Isolate Visual Tweaks: Store the data behind your charts.
The Scripted Plot: Preserve the exact code used to render a graphic.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
section: Rule 10: Providing Public Access to Your Workflow
text:
Rule 10: Providing Public Access to Your Workflow

The Minimum Material: Submit your core data frames and raw source code scripts as mandatory supplementary online files upon publication.
The Review Advantage: Exposing your full workspace infrastructure increases reviewer trust, accelerates editorial turnaround times, and boosts your project’s future citation metrics.
The Open Stance: Always remain prepared to openly answer peer requests for deep architectural or parameter pipeline metrics.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Screens Off, Minds On



Devices Away: Laptops & tablets closed, phones away.
No One Alone: Pair or team up (no solo seats).
Engage Fully: Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 1
Your teammate creates a breathtaking, beautifully styled bar chart for a group presentation. However, when the professor asks to see the 10,000 raw data points that generated the third bar, your teammate sweats and says, “Uh, it’s on my old laptop.”



Can a highly styled chart have any actual academic value?
How should losing access to raw files be treated?
Should the student be accused of data fabrication?





−+
04:00




A pretty chart without raw data trails isn’t science; it’s just creative writing/coding. There is not a lot of academic value in a breathtaking, highly styled chart if the baseline data supporting it cannot be produced on demand.
“The burden of proof.” In some professional environments, an inability to instantly back up a specific visual claim with its underlying numbers looks less like a mistake and more like data fabrication.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 2
A student keeps a beautiful, 100-page handwritten leather notebook. She tracks every single mouse click, every copy-paste action, and every manual data-cleaning step she performs in Excel with flawless precision.



Is the student’s work reproducible?
Is there any value in (or place for) hand-written notes?





−+
04:00




A beautifully kept manual record still fails the core requirement of being an “executable description” that a computer can run and scale.
Manual copy-paste actions and Excel mouse clicks introduce silent, untraceable human errors that version control cannot catch. We should prefer automated scripts that require zero human intervention to repeat.
There is immense value in handwritten notes and manual approaches, but only as a sandbox for human thought, not as the final pipeline for data execution.
The “Why” vs. the “How”: Code is excellent at tracking how a calculation is done, but it is terrible at explaining why you chose to do it. A handwritten notebook is a cognitive sandbox. It is where a researcher maps out messy conceptual logic, sketches potential workflows, and processes failures before writing a single line of script.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 3
You spend three weeks testing a hypothesis on a dataset. Your code is perfect, your pipeline is automated, but the results prove your hypothesis is completely, totally wrong. Your script yields a massive “dead end.”



Did your hypothesis fail, or did you?
Did you just waste 3 weeks of work?
Would you still share your work in a public repo?





−+
04:00





Did your hypothesis fail, or did you? It’s important to separate the quality of your code from the behavior of nature.
Also, an automated “failed” experiment is actually a massive engineering success.
Did you just waste 3 weeks of work? The danger of deleting your dead ends: What happens to the scientific community when researchers hide their failures, forcing the next person to waste weeks re-testing the exact same wrong idea.
Would you still share your work in a public repo? Submit and store it with the exact same reproducibility standards as a success, because documenting “blind alleys” saves future researchers from wasting time on the same mistake.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 4
Your script runs a 4-hour simulation on a large dataset, processing everything live in temporary memory to output a final summary paragraph. When your professor spots an anomaly and asks to see the data right after the initial filtering step, you realize nothing was saved along the way.



What are some advantages of a single “all-or-nothing” live run?
What are some disadvantages of saving intermediate steps?





−+
04:00




Disadvantages of a pipeline that only saves the final answer: impossible to troubleshoot, audit, or verify when a bug or anomaly inevitably appears in the middle.
Discuss the massive waste of time and computational energy that happens when you treat data analysis as a single “all-or-nothing” live run instead of caching milestones.
Debate the engineering trade-off between consuming hard drive space to store temporary milestone files versus consuming hours of processing time to re-run scripts.
Better to transform a 4-hour pipeline into a modular, flexible workflow that can be paused, inspected, and restarted at any point.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll
Be completely honest: When cleaning a dataset or fixing file formatting issues for an assignment, how often do you rely on manual copy-pasting, visual cell edits, or find-and-replace clicks instead of writing a code script?

100% Code Scripted: I never touch the raw file manually; every transformation is written in a reproducible script lines.
The Hybrid Scramble: I try to script, but if a deadline is tight, I secretly open Excel to quickly delete bad rows or copy-paste columns.
Purely Manual: I do almost all data formatting visually using trackpad movements and mouse clicks because it feels faster.
The “I Don’t Track It” Stance: I change cells casually as I work and completely lose track of what I manually edited by the end of the day.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll

You notice a minor discrepancy in plot you generated 3 weeks ago. You need to backtrack to the exact code state that produced that specific figure.
What is the reality of your current local file system?


Perfect Provenance: Every single script modification is systematically frozen in a timestamped Git commit hash; I can jump back in seconds.
The “Folder Vault” Cluster I have copies named script_v1.R, script_v2_fixed.R, and script_final_REAL.R. It will take hours of manual guessing.
The Overwrite Abyss: I continuously modify a single file without saving historical backups. That past code state is permanently gone.
The Cloud Illusion: I assume my background Google Drive/Dropbox sync will save me, even though it doesn’t track execution states.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll
You run a classmate’s random simulation script on your machine using identical data inputs. But they forgot to set a static random seed. Your output values are approximately close (e.g., 84.2% accuracy) but not exactly equal to their published value (84.5%). What is your scientific verdict?

Acceptable Replication: Close enough is good enough for computational science; minor stochastic fluctuations don’t undermine the core theory.
Unverifiable Black Box: An approximate match is a failure; without an exact mathematical match via a random seed, I cannot verify if the pipeline is truly bug-free.
Indifferent Stance: I assume the difference is caused by our different operating system kernels or processor architectures anyway, so a seed won’t fix it.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll
Think about how you write lab reports, group notes, or draft research paragraphs. Where do your conceptual interpretations live relative to the raw output data files that support them?

Fully Welded Documents: I use integrated dynamic document tools (like Quarto or Jupyter Notebooks) so my text and live data logic are locked together natively.
The Absolute Path Blind Bind: I manually type hardcoded server folder paths (e.g., /Users/name/Desktop/run_3) inside a separate Microsoft Word document.
The Total Disconnect: My data lives in a folder on a local server, and my interpretations live entirely in casual emails, Slack chats, or scrap paper notes.

section: 1. Saving Multiple Versions of a File
text:
1. Saving Multiple Versions of a File

A student builds an amazing regression model at 2:00 AM. Exhausted, they save the code as model_final.py.


The next morning, they realize they missed an outlier, tweak the file, and save it as model_final_v2.py.


Two weeks later, their professor asks for a minor adjustment. They end up with model_final_revised_PROFCORRECTED.py.



When looking back at the folder a month later, they have no idea which file generated the actual metrics in their final presentation slide deck.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
2. Hardcoding Absolute Paths

Alex writes a brilliant data cleaning script on his Windows laptop.


He uploads it to a shared folder so his lab partner, Chloe, can run it on her MacBook.


The second Chloe hits execute, the terminal crashes with a fatal File Not Found Error.



The script failed instantly because Chloe’s computer doesn’t have a user named “Alex,” and Mac operating systems don’t even use a C:/ drive design.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
3. Polluting the Global Environment

Maria installs Pandas version 1.5 globally on her laptop to run a machine learning project for a class.


Next semester, she takes an advanced statistics class that requires a new feature only found in Pandas version 2.2. She runs a global upgrade command.



When she tries to re-run her old machine learning code for her portfolio, it completely crashes with syntax errors.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
4. Silent Corruptions

David notices that a few rows in his sensor log dataset contain a typo: "N/A" instead of blank spaces.


He opens the raw file in Microsoft Excel, uses “Find and Replace” to clean them up, hits save, and closes the window.


What he doesn’t realize is that Excel silently reformatted his entire Date column from standard YYYY-MM-DD strings into a localized format like MM/DD/YY, and dropped the leading zeros on all his zip codes.



His Python analysis script now breaks completely because the data was fundamentally altered by a silent software default.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
5. Out-of-Order Executions

Sam is actively prototyping a data chart:

He runs cell 1 to load data,
skips down to cell 10 to drop missing values,
runs cell 4 to alter a variable,
and then jumps back to cell 2 to plot the results.



The graph looks perfect. He saves the notebook and emails it to his professor.


The professor opens the file, hits “Run All Cells” from top to bottom, and gets an entirely different chart with a broken trendline.



The perfect result only existed because of the chaotic, invisible memory sequence trapped inside Sam’s live session.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
6. Dangers of Copy-Pasting

Elena computes a critical p-value for her research paper: 0.00412. She opens her jupyter notebook, and types it in.


Later that week, she realizes her input data had duplicated rows, so she runs the script again. The new correct p-value changes to 0.0412.


Because the report is a completely detached text file, she forgets to update the document manually.



She accidentally publishes a report with a massive typo that completely flips the statistical significance of her research.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
7. Unrepeatable Breakthroughs

A student builds a fraud-detection model that achieves an impressive 95% accuracy score.


Excitedly, she calls her supervisor over to show them the breakthrough. She hits execution again to demonstrate the live pipeline.


The accuracy drops to 89%. She runs it a third time, and it jumps to 92%.



Because she forgot to hardcode a random seed marker (numpy.random.seed(42)), the dataset splits randomly on every execution, rendering her breakthrough metrics entirely un-reproducible.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
8. The Interactive GUI Trap

Kevin uses a graphical enterprise software program to clean a dataset, clicking visual buttons to remove columns, drop null rows, and filter outliers.


He exports a beautiful chart for a corporate presentation.


Six months later, a regulatory compliance officer demands an audit trail detailing exactly why certain outlier rows were dropped from the dataset.



Because Kevin handled the entire process through manual mouse clicks inside a black-box GUI rather than writing a programmatic script, he has no way to prove or replicate his step-by-step logic, putting the validity of the entire project at risk.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
9. The Single-Commit Mega-Upload

Ryan works diligently on an assignment for three weeks without committing a single line of code.


On Sunday night, he runs git add . and git commit -m "fixed project stuff", pushing the entire thing to GitHub.


On Monday morning, his professor points out that a code adjustment made on day 4 accidentally ruined the data integrity pipeline.



Because Ryan mashed 21 days of complex, erratic file changes into a single history node, he cannot roll back the graph to isolate the error, forcing him to manually untangle his entire codebase.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
10. The “Free Real Estate” Licensing Illusion

An open-source research team discovers a student’s public repository containing a clever, highly optimized data parsing code.


They want to integrate it into a medical framework that could save lives, but their legal compliance department blocks it completely.


Because the student forgot to include an explicit LICENSE file (like MIT or Apache 2.0), the code legally defaults to strict, restrictive copyright ownership.



The useful pipeline remains legally locked away from helping the community.

AI Tools policy
We strongly encourage you to focus on independent learning and original problem-solving. At the same time, we recognize that generative AI tools are an increasingly standard part of modern workflows. We are not banning AI tools in this course, as doing so is neither realistic nor desirable.
This course is designed to help you build fundamental skills, judgment, and deep understanding—outcomes AI cannot achieve for you. Our main goal is to foster transparency and genuine engagement with the material, aligning with the core philosophy of STAT 159/259.
Core Expectations 

Do the thinking yourself. Use AI to support your learning, not replace it. If a tool handles the core reasoning, drafting, or problem-solving while you merely copy and submit the output, you are missing out on learning the material.
Disclose your usage. If you use AI tools on an assignment—whether for brainstorming, debugging code, editing text, checking work, or drafting—you must state so explicitly. A short note on your assignment is sufficient: include the tool and version used (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-4o), what you used it for, the primary prompts used, and where it was applied.


Why this matters: Transparency aligns directly with the collaborative and reproducible data science practices central to this course. Openly documenting how work was produced ensures your workflow can be evaluated and built upon by others.


Understand everything you submit. You are fully accountable for all submitted work. If you include AI-generated code, text, or figures, you must be able to explain, defend, and walk through them as if you created them entirely yourself. If you cannot explain a line of code or a specific claim, do not submit it.
Violations of the course AI policy:

Undisclosed AI Use: Submitting AI-assisted or AI-generated work without clear disclosure.
Lack of Comprehension: Submitting AI-generated work that you cannot explain, defend, or demonstrate understanding of when asked.


The ultimate objective of this course isn’t just to produce correct answers; it is to build critical thinking, master modern tools, and communicate complex ideas clearly. Using AI responsibly and transparently is part of developing those professional skills.

1. Reflecting on Reproducible
The Turing Way defines a “reproducible” result as using the same data and the same analysis steps. Think back to a programming or data assignment you submitted in a previous semester.
If your laptop was lost today and you had to reconstruct that project on a classmate’s machine using only your memory and the files currently backed up in your email/cloud, what are the exact “ghosts” (a hidden file path, an unrecorded package version, an un-downloaded dataset) that would cause the reproduction to completely fail?


2. Reflecting on Robust
A result is “robust” if using different analysis steps on the same data yields a qualitatively identical answer (e.g., swapping from an R package to a Python script).
If you were forced to completely rewrite your favorite data script into a programming language you barely know, which specific part of your code’s logic do you suspect would fall apart or yield a different mathematical rounding result, and why?


3. Reproducible Failure
Imagine a peer creates a messy, un-versioned script that accidentally discovers a brilliant, groundbreaking pattern in a public dataset, but their workflow is completely un-reproducible.
You build a flawless, fully automated, version-controlled pipeline that proves a hypothesis is completely wrong, but anyone can rerun it perfectly. In your own words, defend why your “reproducible failure” might actually be more valuable to the progress of science than their “sloppy success.”

title: UNIX Part 1
text:
Important File Concepts

Everything is a File (including directories)
Folder = Directory
No concept of “disk”
At any given time we are inside a directory
The current directory is the working directory
From that directory we can move up or down

title: UNIX Part 1
text:
Special Directories
Root directory: the top-level folder in a computer’s file system, acting as the main starting point from which all other directories and files branch out, similar to the trunk of a tree.


Home directory: a user’s personal folder in a multi-user operating system that holds their private files, settings, and data, acting as their default workspace upon login.


Working directory: the specific folder in a computer’s file system where a user is currently working or where a process is executing commands.

title: UNIX Part 1

File Paths
Each file and directory has a unique name in the filesystem called a path.



File paths can be specified in 2 ways:

Absolute Paths: always from the root directory.
Relative Paths: location relative to a working directory.

title: UNIX Part 1
section: Example: What happens when you create a folder?
text:
Example: What happens when you create a folder?
Command like mkdir Photos

The Shell’s Job: You type mkdir Photos into your terminal. The shell reads this text, realizes you want to run the “make directory” program, and translates your request into a standard system request (a system call).
The Handshake: The shell passes this request across the boundary to the kernel.
The Kernel’s Job: The kernel receives the request. It checks if you have permission to modify the storage. It then talks directly to your Hard Drive or SSD, physically carving out space on the disk to save your new “Photos” folder.

title: UNIX Part 1
text:

The Operating System is the entire restaurant.
The Shell is the waiter. It takes your order (commands) and translates it.
The Kernel is the kitchen staff. They actually handle the raw ingredients (hardware, memory) and cook the food.
Notice: The waiter doesn’t talk to “the restaurant”—the waiter talks to the kitchen.

There’s one root commit (initial commit)

Unix file naming

Maximum of 255 characters
Avoid most symbols: \ / * & % ? $ | ^ ~ < >
Use A-Z, a-z, 0-9, period, underscore, hyphen
Don’t use a hyphen - as the first character

Good idea to use file extensions

Spend time planning out both folder hierarchy and file naming conventions in the beginning of a project.
Consider how you or others will look for and access files at a later date.

title: Naming Files
text:
1) What information (metadata) is important?

Ideally, pick three pieces of metadata; use no more than five.
This metadata should be enough for you to visually scan the file names and easily understand what’s in each one.
Example: For my images, I want to know date, sample ID, and image number for that sample on that date.

title: Naming Files
section: 2) Do you need to abbreviate any of the metadata or encode it?
text:
2) Do you need to abbreviate any of the metadata or encode it?

If any of the metadata from step 1 is described by lots of text, decide what shortened information to keep.
If any of the metadata from step 1 has regular categories, standardize the categories and/or replace them with 2- or 3-letter codes; be sure to document these codes.
Example: Sample ID will use a code made up of: a 2-letter project abbreviation (project 1 = P1, project 2 = P2); a 3-letter species abbreviation (mouse = “MUS”, fruit fly = “DRS”); and 3-digit sample ID (assigned in my notebook).

title: Naming Files
section: 3) What is the order for the metadata in the file name?
text:
3) What is the order for the metadata in the file name?

Think about how you want to sort and search for your files to decide what metadata should appear at the beginning of the file name.
If date is important, use ISO 8601-formatted dates (YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD) at the beginning of the file names so dates sort chronologically.
Example 1: My sample ID is most important so I will list it first, followed by date, then image number

title: Naming Files
section: 4) What characters will you use to separate each piece of metadata in the file name?
text:
4) What characters will you use to separate each piece of metadata in the file name?

Many computer systems cannot handle spaces in file names.
To make file names both computer- and human-readable, use dashes (-), underscores (_), and/or capitalize the first letter of each word in the file names.
Example: I will use underscores to separate metadata and dashes between parts of my sample ID.

title: Naming Files
section: 5) Will you need to track different versions of each file?
text:
5) Will you need to track different versions of each file?

You can track versions of a file by appending version information to end of the file name.
Consider using a version number (e.g. v01) or the version date (use ISO 8601 format: YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD).
Example: As each image goes through my analysis workflow, I will append the version type to the end of the file name (e.g. _raw, _processed, and _composite)

title: Naming Files
section: 6) Write down your naming convention pattern.
text:
6) Write down your naming convention pattern.

Make sure the convention only uses alphanumeric characters, dashes, and underscores. Ideally, file names will be 32 characters or less.
Example: my file naming convention is

SA-MPL-EID_YYYYMMDD_###_status.tif

Examples are P1-MUS023_20200229_051_raw.tif and P2-DRS-285_20191031_062_composite.tif
